title: What the homepage has to prove for a small clinic
metaTitle: Small clinic homepage: room, clinician, booking
excerpt: A small clinic homepage should show the room and the clinician, then offer a way to book a visit. A stock smile and a procedure list do not do that job.
alt: Clothes on wooden hangers suspended from a white branch against a plain wall, a few real objects in plain view for a homepage that should show the room rather than a costume.
caption: Clothes on hangers against a plain wall. The first screen should be this literal. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a small clinic put on the first screen?
faqs.answer: Show the room or the clinician, say what the first visit is, and offer a way to book. Add the address or the neighborhood if people travel to you. A patient who is already anxious needs those facts before a slogan. A procedure menu can wait until they know where they would be walking in.

faqs.question: Should the homepage list every service?
faqs.answer: No. A long procedure list makes an anxious patient feel they must self-diagnose before they are allowed to book. Name the visits you want them to recognize, in their words, and link deeper pages for the rest. The homepage's job is the room, the clinician, and the booking.

faqs.question: Where should the phone number live?
faqs.answer: On the first screen, as text a person can tap, next to the booking button. Some patients will not trust a form on a hard day. The number should be the clinic's real front desk, with the hours beside it. A number buried in the footer is a number many people will not find.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A small clinic homepage has one job for a patient who is already anxious. Show the room and the clinician, and offer a way to book a visit.

Stock smiles and a procedure list fail that patient. A grin from a photo library does not show where they will sit. A menu of treatments asks them to diagnose themselves before they know if they are in the right place. Write the page in this order: room, clinician, booking.

## The room, before the welcome

The first screen should answer a physical question. Where would I be? A waiting room with the chairs you actually have. A treatment room with the light you actually use. The door from the street, if the street is how people arrive. Patients who are nervous are often rehearsing the arrival. Give them the arrival.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on visits is a useful constraint. People often leave a page within 10 to 20 seconds, and a page earns more of their time only when the value is clear in about 10 seconds. For a clinic, the value is not a motto about compassionate care. It is the place and the person. If the hero is a stock photograph of a smile, those seconds are spent wondering whether the clinic is real.

Put a short sentence on the picture. Who you see, and what the first visit is for. "A first visit for back pain with Dr. Shah, in a single treatment room on George Street" is a sentence a person can use. "Welcome to a new standard of wellness" is a sentence they cannot picture. The sentence should still work if the image is slow to load, because some patients will be on a phone in a car park.

Show hours and the neighborhood in the same first view if you can do it in one line. Anxiety grows when the practical facts are treated as footer material. People decide whether they can get there before they decide whether they like your typeface.

## The clinician, with a responsibility

Name the person they will see. A small clinic's advantage is that the name is knowable. Use it. Role, and the kind of visit they lead. A portrait from your room, not a headshot that could belong to a dental advert in another city. If several clinicians share the work, say how a patient is matched. "You will see whoever is on the book that morning" is a fact. Hide it and the homepage is smoother and less honest.

Google's helpful-content guidance treats trust as the center of experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness, and it gives extra weight to topics that can affect someone's health. A clinic homepage is that kind of page. A visitor should be able to tell who is offering the care. A logo and a stock smile do not answer. A name and a room do.

Credentials belong when they change the decision to book. The registration, the years in this kind of work, the hospital or training that matters to this patient. A ribbon of badges does not. Write the one fact your front desk already says on the phone. If the front desk cannot say it simply, it is not ready for the hero.

If a nurse, a therapist, or a front-desk lead is who the patient will meet first, name that person too. "You will check in with Sam, and the clinician will be Dr. Shah" is a map of the hour. Maps reduce anxiety more than adjectives do.

## One path: book the visit

The button should say "Book a visit," or a plainer variant that names the visit. "Book a first visit for back pain." It should be visible next to the room and the name, and it should be a real booking, not a scroll to a paragraph. If you cannot take bookings online yet, the button can call the desk, and the label should say "Call to book." Do not label a phone call as a portal.

Say what the patient will be asked, in one line. A name, a phone number, and the reason for the visit are enough to start. Insurance details can be the next step if you truly need them before you can confirm. Asking for a full history in the hero form is how a nervous person closes the tab. The homepage is the decision to book, not the intake packet.

Repeat the path after the practical facts, in the same words. Add the phone number beside it, as text. Some patients will not submit a form when they are upset or in pain. The number is not a failure of the design. It is the other honest door. Put hours next to it so they know whether a human will answer.

Do not compete with the booking. "Download our app," "Join the newsletter," and "Take a quiz" are other jobs. They can exist later for people who already know you. On the first screen they split a person who came to do one difficult thing.

## Why a procedure list fails the first screen

A procedure list feels responsible to the clinic. It proves range. To an anxious patient it reads as a test. They scan for the word they fear, or they cannot find their word and assume they should not call. Either result delays the booking the page was for.

If you offer several kinds of visit, name three in the patient's language, under the fold, each with a sentence about who it is for and a link to book that visit. "First visit." "A follow-up." "A question before you book." That is a map. Forty treatment names in a grid is a catalog. Catalogs belong on a services page with boundaries, not on the door.

Stock smiles fail for a related reason. They are not the room and they are not the clinician. A patient can feel the swap. The page says "care" and shows a person who does not work there. Google's people-first test asks whether you demonstrate first-hand experience. A photograph of your own room is that demonstration. A rented smile is the opposite.

Before-and-after pictures are a separate refusal on the homepage. They shock, they over-promise, and they make the first screen about an outcome you may not be allowed to imply. If a clinical result is something you are permitted to show, it belongs in a considered proof page with context, not in a carousel above the booking button.

## Practical facts that calm

After the room, the name, and the booking, add the facts a patient is already worrying about. Keep each one short.

- Where you are, and how to arrive. A step, an elevator, a car park, a bus stop.
- How long a first visit usually takes, if you know.
- What to bring. A referral if you require one. A list of medicines. Comfortable clothes if that is true.
- What the visit will not be. No procedure on the first day, if that is true. No surprise that they came for a conversation and were taken into a treatment.
- The shape of the fee. A first visit has a fee, insurance may cover part of it, the desk will say before you come. Do not hide a knowable number if the desk quotes it every day.

These lines are the care. A paragraph about your philosophy is optional and usually worse. Patients in pain are not looking for a worldview. They are looking for a door they can open.

Write the access facts even when they are imperfect. "There are two steps at the entrance, and a bell if you need help with the door" is more trustworthy than silence. Silence makes people arrive and discover the limit in public, which is a harder moment than reading it at home.

## What to remove from the hero

Cut anything that does not show the room, the clinician, or the booking.

- A video that plays before the room is visible.
- A slider of stock families.
- Three slogans stacked on the picture.
- A chat window that covers "Book a visit."
- Awards and association logos with no sentence.
- The word "welcome" as the whole headline.

Hanabi builds marketing sites in Next.js, with the layout in Tailwind, and keeps motion quiet enough that a button does not move while the page settles. A clinic homepage should be calmer than a product launch. The patient is not here to be impressed. They are here to see if they can come in.

Read the hero on a phone, outside, with the brightness down. That is the visit. If the room is a blur and the button is below an essay, redesign the stack. Desktop can add a wider view of the same room. It should not invent a different story.

## Review it with someone who is nervous

Ask a friend who has booked a clinic while worried, not a colleague who knows the services by heart. Give them the phone. Ask what the place is, who they would see, and how they would book. If they start reading procedures aloud, the list has taken over. If they say "they seem nice," you have a mood and not a homepage.

Then call the number yourself. The voice that answers should match the page. If the page promises online booking and the phone says "we do not use that," fix the page today. A mismatch at the door is the fastest way to confirm someone's anxiety.

When you want a second pair of eyes on that first screen, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The work is a site that shows the real room and a real next step, designed and built so the booking is not a plugin shouting over the photograph.

The next page this patient opens, if they are still unsure, is often the price. [A pricing page for a small clinic](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-small-clinic) is about showing what the visit includes, what it does not, and how to book without turning the fee into a guessing game.
